result.markdown: --- title: "Observation models and simulated data" course-unit: ch07-observation-models status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - Every earlier chapter built a **process model**: rules that generate the latent epidemic trajectory. - Surveillance data are never the latent process — they are **noisy, partial counts**. - An **observation model** links the two, and is the raw material for the inference chapters that follow. ::: {.notes} Keep the process/observation split explicit. Chapters 8 and 9 both estimate the same process parameters *through* this observation layer, so the modelling choices made here propagate directly into the inference results. ::: ## Process and observation, side by side Baseline SIR with a cumulative-incidence state $C$ ($S_0=990, I_0=10, R_0=0, N=1000, c=10, \beta=0.05, \gamma=0.25$): $$ \dot S=-\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N},\quad \dot I=\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,\quad \dot R=\gamma I,\quad \dot C=\beta c\tfrac{SI}{N}. $$ | | Process | Observation | |---|---|---| | Determinism | deterministic | stochastic | | Time | continuous | discrete (daily) | | State | densities $S,I,R,C$ | counts $Y_t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ | ::: {.notes} Only *new* infections generate reports, so the signal is incidence, not prevalence. The latent daily incidence is the increment of $C$. ::: ## Count models: Poisson vs negative-binomial Latent incidence $x_t=C(t)-C(t-1)$; reporting fraction $\rho$: $$ Y_t\mid x_t\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\rho x_t),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_t]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_t]=\rho x_t, $$ $$ Y_t\mid x_t\sim\operatorname{NegBin}\!\Big(r,\tfrac{r}{r+\rho x_t}\Big),\quad \operatorname{Var}[Y_t]=\rho x_t+\tfrac{(\rho x_t)^2}{r}. $$ Poisson is **equidispersed**; the negative-binomial adds overdispersion and recovers Poisson as $r\to\infty$. ::: {.notes} Real surveillance is almost always overdispersed because of batching, weekday effects, and super-spreading. The dispersion $r$ is the one extra parameter that buys a defensible variance. ::: ## Simulating case reports ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch07-obs .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch07-obs .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Latent daily incidence (line) with one Poisson (left) and one overdispersed negative-binomial (right) realisation. Same latent mean, wider negative-binomial scatter. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Each observation model gets its own `StableRNG` so the streams are independent and reproducible. The full book chapter also derives incidence with a `PresetTimeCallback` reset and a delay differential equation, and prefers plain differencing for downstream inference. ::: ## Validation and dispersion ::: {#cell-ch07-validation .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#ch07-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (conservation_error = 5.5e-13, poisson_var_over_mean = 0.98, negbin_var_over_mean = 5.54) ``` ::: ::: - **Conservation:** $C(t)=S_0-S(t)$ to solver tolerance. - At the peak, **replicate** Poisson counts are equidispersed ($\text{var}/\text{mean}\approx1$); negative-binomial counts are overdispersed. ::: {.notes} Dispersion must be measured across *replicates at a fixed time*, not along the time series, whose spread reflects the epidemic curve. Averaging thousands of Poisson realisations back to the latent mean is the book chapter's third check. ::: ## Julia API ```julia using EpiModelingCourse # sir_cumulative_ode!, synthetic_incidence df = synthetic_incidence(; seed = 1, tspan = (0.0, 40.0), observation_noise = :poisson, reporting_rate = 1.0) using Distributions # Poisson, NegativeBinomial using StableRNGs # StableRNG(seed) for reproducible streams ``` - `OrdinaryDiffEq` integrates the cumulative-incidence ODE. - `Distributions` supplies the count models; `StableRNG` fixes the seed. ::: {.notes} The course package `synthetic_incidence` returns a stable-schema `DataFrame` (`time, S, I, R, cumulative_incidence, incidence, expected_incidence, observed_incidence`) so the chapter, slides and notebook share one generator. ::: ## Takeaways and limitations - Separate the **latent process** from the **observation process**. - Poisson understates uncertainty when reporting is clustered; use the negative-binomial. - $\rho$ and $\beta$ both scale the mean $\Rightarrow$ **not identifiable** from one incidence series (Chapter 10). - We assumed instantaneous, conditionally independent reporting — real systems add delays and weekday effects. Read the [book chapter](../../chapters/07-observation-models.html); see [Distributions.jl](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/) and [StableRNGs.jl](https://github.com/JuliaRandom/StableRNGs.jl). ::: {.notes} Close by previewing the two inference chapters: Chapter 8 estimates parameters by maximum likelihood from these reports, Chapter 9 by Bayesian sampling. :::
